additions.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, section 66A: Misconduct: action by the FCA
additions.quote: did not take such steps as a person in the senior manager's position could reasonably be expected to take to avoid the contravention occurring
additions.why: The statutory 'duty of responsibility' behind the senior managers regime: a senior manager responsible for an area where the firm breaks a rule is personally liable to regulatory action unless they took reasonable steps. This is the binding rule that makes a named owner matter in financial services. Applies to authorised firms only; it does not mention AI; section 66B is the equivalent for the Prudential Regulation Authority. Revised text, shown as up to date to 5 October 2026.

additions.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
additions.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
additions.locator: Executive summary, 'Governance and accountability'; section 3.1 (Governance and accountability), 'Accountability'
additions.quote: accountability is often split with most firms reporting three or more accountable persons or bodies
additions.why: UK survey evidence on who owns AI in practice: 84% of firms using AI reported an accountable person for their AI framework and 72% placed accountability for use cases with executive leadership, yet accountability was commonly split three or more ways. Later than the 2022 discussion paper the brief relies on. Voluntary survey of 118 regulated financial firms; self-reported; financial services only.

additions.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
additions.locator: 'How should we approach AI governance and risk management?', second and third paragraphs
additions.quote: You cannot delegate these issues to data scientists or engineering teams.
additions.why: The data protection regulator's statement that accountability for AI rests with senior management and cannot be passed down to technical teams, and that roles and responsibilities maps must be aligned to the AI governance strategy. Guidance, not law; marked 'under review' following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; data protection only.

additions.title: Three lines of defense against risks from AI
additions.publisher: Jonas Schuett (arXiv; published in AI & Society)
additions.quote: It is a risk management framework that helps organizations to assign and coordinate risk management roles and responsibilities.
additions.why: Research applying the three lines model to AI: who owns the risk, who challenges, who assures, and how that closes gaps where nobody is responsible. Author's arXiv copy of an article later published in AI & Society (doi 10.1007/s00146-023-01811-0); the journal copy could not be read (publisher blocked automated reading). Conceptual, not empirical, and written about companies that develop AI.

additions.title: Putting AI Ethics into Practice: The Hourglass Model of Organizational AI Governance
additions.publisher: Matti Mäntymäki, Matti Minkkinen, Teemu Birkstedt and Mika Viljanen (arXiv)
additions.locator: Section on the AI system layer, component F 'Accountability and ownership' (tasks T54-T56), PDF p.9
additions.quote: Ensuring necessary decision rights and responsibilities to govern the AI system and its algorithmic components
additions.why: Research framework that makes 'accountability and ownership' a required component of governing each AI system, with a head of AI, a system owner and an algorithm owner named. Supports allocating decision rights per system, not only at the top. Preprint (version 2, 31 January 2023; the arXiv page gives no journal reference); a framework developed with practitioners, not a test of outcomes; aligned to a draft of the EU AI Act.

rejected.title: Springer journal copies (AI & Society, Philosophy & Technology, AI and Ethics, Minds and Machines)
rejected.reason: Blocked: link.springer.com returned a 'Client Challenge' page to every request (four articles tried). Not bypassed. Where the author's own arXiv copy exists it was read instead; Novelli, Taddeo and Floridi on accountability, Santoni de Sio and Mecacci on responsibility gaps, and Mantymaki et al. on defining organisational AI governance were not read and are not cited.

rejected.title: Raji et al., Closing the AI Accountability Gap (arXiv 2001.00973)
rejected.reason: Abstract read. About internal audit across the development life cycle, not named ownership or escalation; left for the assurance criterion.

rejected.title: Cobbe, Lee and Singh, Reviewable Automated Decision-Making (arXiv 2102.04201)
rejected.reason: Abstract read. About record-keeping for review, not decision rights; left for the evidence-trail criterion.

rejected.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 17(1)(m), accountability framework
rejected.reason: Read. Relevant, but this criterion already cites the Act (Article 26); Article 17 is used under policy architecture instead.

rejected.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making
rejected.reason: Lead check 5 Oct 2026: the site refuses automated reading (HTTP 403), so the quotation cannot be machine-checked. Dropped.

brief_check: Nothing contradicts the brief. One point dates it slightly: the brief cites the regulators' 2022 discussion paper; their November 2024 survey (118 firms) reports 84% with an accountable person for their AI framework and 72% allocating accountability to executive leadership, with accountability often split three or more ways (executive summary and section 3.1).
